sections.title: A kitchen that never closes
sections.intro_md:
Walk into the **Guru Ram Das Langar** at the Golden Temple in Amritsar at almost any hour and you join a queue for a free meal. You take a steel plate, sit cross-legged on a long jute mat in a row called a **pangat**, and volunteers come down the line with dal, a vegetable, kheer and rotis pressed into your cupped hands. Nobody asks your religion, caste or name. On an ordinary day the kitchen serves more than **100,000 meals**; on festival days, far more.

The rule is five centuries old. Guru Nanak, born in 1469, made shared eating a statement against caste, and the third Guru, Amar Das, is remembered for insisting that even the Mughal emperor Akbar sit on the floor and eat with everyone before meeting him.

That is Punjab in one scene: open-handed, organised, proud, and built on food. The paradox sits outside the city. The same fields that filled India's granaries after 1965 are now pumping groundwater faster than the rain can return it.

data.label: Meals a day at the langar

spotlights.name: Harmandir Sahib (the Golden Temple)
spotlights.spot_it: A small two-storey shrine covered in gold, sitting in the middle of a square pool, reached by a single causeway.
spotlights.story_md: Guru Arjan began the shrine in **1581** beside a pool dug by his father, Guru Ram Das, and installed the first copy of the Adi Granth inside on **16 August 1604**. Unlike most temples, it sits **lower** than the city around it: you walk down steps to reach it, a lesson in humility. It has **four doors**, one on each side, to say it is open to all four directions and every caste. The marble and gold you see came later: Maharaja Ranjit Singh rebuilt it in marble and copper in 1809 and had it covered in gold leaf in 1830. The pool, the **Amrit Sarovar**, is about 150 m square and 5 m deep.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the spiritual centre of the world's roughly 25 to 30 million Sikhs.
spotlights.memory_hook: A golden house of God that you walk down into, with a door on every side.

spotlights.name: Langar, the free community kitchen
spotlights.spot_it: Rows of people of every kind sitting on the floor, eating the same food off steel plates, served by volunteers.
spotlights.story_md: Every gurdwara in the world runs a langar, but Amritsar's is the biggest. Volunteers, many of them visitors who simply walk in, chop onions, roll rotis and wash plates in a chain that never stops. Machines now help: a roti press can turn out thousands an hour, and huge cauldrons of dal are stirred with paddles. The food is vegetarian so that no one, of any faith, is excluded. The rule of sitting in a line on the floor, the **pangat**, is the point: the rich and the poor, the high caste and the low, eat level with each other. During the 2020 to 2021 farmers' protests and many disasters since, Sikh groups have set up langars on highways and in flood zones.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turned the shared meal into a weapon against caste, and still feeds strangers at scale.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sit on the floor, hold out your hands: in Amritsar the meal comes to you, whoever you are.

sections.title: Punjab at a glance
sections.intro_md:
The name is Persian: **panj** (five) and **āb** (waters), the land of five rivers. The five were the Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej. In 1947 the Radcliffe Line gave the western three-fifths of the old province to Pakistan, and in 1966 Indian Punjab was cut again to make **Haryana** and to add its hill districts to **Himachal Pradesh**. What is left is a compact plain of **50,362 km²**, about 1.5% of India's land, with only the Sutlej and Beas wholly inside it and the Ravi along its northern edge.

Census 2011 counted **2,77,43,338** people. It is the only state where **Sikhs** are the majority, **57.7%**, with Hindus at 38.5%. It also has India's highest share of **Scheduled Castes**, **31.9%**. Its sex ratio, **895** women per 1,000 men in 2011, was among the worst in India, a scar of sex-selective abortion that has slowly improved since.

Punjab has **23 districts**, a 117-seat assembly and no capital of its own: **Chandigarh**, a union territory, serves both Punjab and Haryana. People still speak of three old regions named by rivers: **Majha** between the Ravi and Beas, **Doaba** between the Beas and Sutlej, and **Malwa** south of the Sutlej.

spotlights.name: Chandigarh and the Capitol Complex
spotlights.spot_it: Raw concrete government buildings with sweeping roofs, set across a vast open plaza with a giant metal hand on a pole.
spotlights.story_md: When Lahore went to Pakistan, East Punjab lost its capital. Nehru wanted a new city 'unfettered by the traditions of the past', and in 1951 the Swiss-French architect **Le Corbusier** took over the plan. He laid the city out in rectangular **sectors** of about 800 m by 1,200 m, each meant to be a walkable neighbourhood, and designed the **Capitol Complex**: the High Court, the Secretariat and the Legislative Assembly, all in bare concrete. Its symbol is the **Open Hand**, a 26 m tall metal hand that turns in the wind, meant to say 'open to give, open to receive'. In 2016 the Capitol Complex became part of a UNESCO World Heritage listing of Le Corbusier's work across seven countries.
spotlights.why_it_matters: India's first planned city after independence, and still a capital shared by two states.
spotlights.memory_hook: A city drawn on a grid by a Swiss architect, ruled by a giant open hand.

spotlights.name: Majha, Doaba and Malwa
spotlights.when: Old regional names, still used daily
spotlights.spot_it: Majha around Amritsar, Doaba around Jalandhar, Malwa from Ludhiana to Bathinda: ask a Punjabi which they are from.
spotlights.story_md: **Majha**, the land between the Ravi and the Beas around Amritsar and Gurdaspur, is the old Sikh heartland; its people are called Majhails. **Doaba**, the wedge between the Beas and the Sutlej around Jalandhar and Hoshiarpur, has the most emigrants: whole villages here have relatives in England and Canada, and the remittances show in large houses. **Malwa**, everything south of the Sutlej from Ludhiana to Bathinda and Patiala, is the biggest, with about two-thirds of the assembly seats, and so decides elections. It was once the dry cotton country of the princely states. A fourth small area, **Puadh**, lies around Chandigarh and Ropar. Each region has its own accent of Punjabi.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The three regions still shape accents, migration, politics and stereotypes.
spotlights.memory_hook: Majha is the Golden Temple, Doaba is the airport, Malwa is the ballot box.

sections.title: Rivers, doabs and a flat green plate
sections.intro_md:
Punjab is one of the flattest, most fertile pieces of land on Earth. Rivers coming down from the Himalaya dropped silt here for millions of years, and the plain falls only about 200 m across the whole state, from around 300 m near Pathankot to about 180 m in the south-west. The land between two rivers is called a **doab**; Punjab is a set of them.

The only hills are the **Shivaliks**, a low, crumbly range along the north-eastern edge in Hoshiarpur, Ropar and Pathankot districts. The belt below them, the **Kandi**, is cut by seasonal streams called **chos** that flood in the monsoon and are dry the rest of the year. Natural forest is scarce: Punjab's forest cover is under 4% of its area, among the lowest of any state.

Water arrives from outside. Dams in the hills, **Bhakra**, **Pong** and **Ranjit Sagar**, store it and feed the canals; when they release floods at once, as in 2025, the plain goes under.

spotlights.name: Harike Wetland
spotlights.spot_it: A wide shallow lake of reeds and water hyacinth where the Beas meets the Sutlej, crowded with ducks in winter.
spotlights.story_md: Harike was made by accident. A barrage built in **1953** at the meeting point of the **Beas and Sutlej** to feed canals backed the water up into a shallow lake of about 41 km². It became the largest wetland in northern India and was named a **Ramsar** wetland of international importance in 1990. In winter, ducks and geese arrive from Central Asia and Siberia, often tens of thousands at once. From Harike the giant **Indira Gandhi Canal** carries water some 650 km into the Thar desert of Rajasthan. The lake also catches the dirt of upstream cities, and campaigners have long fought over the black water of the Buddha Nullah from Ludhiana.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The wetland is both a bird sanctuary and the tap that waters the Rajasthan desert.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two rivers meet, a dam hiccups, and Siberian ducks get a winter home.

spotlights.name: Indus river dolphin (bulhan)
spotlights.spot_it: A grey, long-beaked river dolphin that surfaces with a short puff; it is almost blind.
spotlights.story_md: The Indus river dolphin has no proper lens in its eyes and finds its food by echolocation, swimming on its side along the riverbed. Almost the entire species, about **2,000** animals, lives in Pakistan's Indus. A tiny, isolated group survives in India in a stretch of the **Beas** between Talwara and Harike, cut off from the rest by barrages. Surveys have found only a handful here: estimates range from about 5 to 11 animals in earlier counts down to **3** in a 2024 Wildlife Institute of India estimate. Punjab named the dolphin its **state aquatic animal**, and the Beas stretch is a conservation reserve. Locals call it **bulhan**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of the rarest mammals in India, a whole population that could vanish in our lifetime.
spotlights.memory_hook: A blind dolphin in a Punjab river, navigating by sound, with almost no one left to call to.

sections.title: Before the Gurus: 5,000 years on the plain
sections.intro_md:
The great Harappan city of **Harappa** stands on the Ravi in what is now Pakistani Punjab, but the Indus civilisation reached deep into the Indian side too. At **Ropar** on the Sutlej, archaeologists in the 1950s found the first Harappan site excavated in independent India.

The **Rig Veda**, the oldest Sanskrit text, was composed largely in this land of rivers, which it called **Sapta Sindhu**, the seven rivers. Its hymns name the Shutudri (Sutlej), Vipash (Beas) and Parushni (Ravi). Every invader from the north-west came through Punjab: Persians, Greeks, Kushans, Huns, Ghaznavids, Ghurids, Mughals and Afghans. That is why Punjabis say their land was 'the sword arm and the doorway' of India.

In **326 BCE** Alexander of Macedon reached the Beas. His exhausted army refused to go further east, and he turned back. Later the Kushans left Buddhist stupas and sculpture at **Sanghol**, and the Delhi Sultanate fortified **Bathinda** on the old route to the west.

spotlights.name: Alexander turns back at the Beas
spotlights.spot_it: Today just the Beas itself, wide and braided as it leaves the hills near Pathankot.
spotlights.story_md: After eight years and about 18,000 km of marching from Macedonia, Alexander's army reached the **Hyphasis**, the Greek name for the Beas, in **326 BCE**. Ahead lay the Ganges plain and rumours of the huge armies of the Nanda kings. The soldiers, worn out by monsoon rain, refused to cross. Alexander sulked in his tent for three days, then gave in. According to the Greek historians he built **twelve giant altars** on the bank to mark the furthest point of his empire. No trace of them has been found. The Beas, a river many Punjabis cross without a thought, is where the ancient world's most famous conquest ran out.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the eastern edge of Alexander's empire, and it lies in Punjab.
spotlights.memory_hook: The world's greatest general beaten not by an army but by his own men, at the Beas.

sections.title: Ten Gurus, one book
sections.intro_md:
Sikhism is the youngest of the major world religions and was born here. Its founder, **Guru Nanak** (1469 to 1539), taught that there is one God, **Ik Onkar**, beyond any religion's name, and that a good life means three things: **naam japna** (remembering God), **kirat karni** (honest work) and **vand chhakna** (sharing what you have). He rejected caste, idol worship and the idea that holiness requires leaving family life.

Nine Gurus followed him. The fifth, **Arjan**, compiled the scripture and built the Harmandir; he was executed by the Mughals in 1606. The ninth, **Tegh Bahadur**, was beheaded in Delhi in 1675. The tenth, **Gobind Singh**, created the **Khalsa** in 1699 and, before his death in 1708, declared that after him the Guru would be the scripture itself, the **Guru Granth Sahib**.

Punjab is also home to other faiths with deep local roots: the **Ravidassia** community, which reveres the 15th-century saint Ravidas; **Qadian**, birthplace of the Ahmadiyya movement; and **Malerkotla**, a Muslim-majority town that Sikhs regard with special gratitude.

spotlights.name: Guru Nanak
spotlights.spot_it: In paintings: a white-bearded man in a simple robe and turban, often with Bhai Mardana playing the rabab beside him.
spotlights.story_md: Nanak was born to a Hindu accountant's family in **Talwandi**, now Nankana Sahib in Pakistan. After an experience at the river Bein around 1499, he announced 'there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim' and set out on long journeys, the **udasis**, said to have taken him to Assam, Sri Lanka, Tibet and Mecca, always with his Muslim companion **Bhai Mardana**, who played the rabab while Nanak sang. He did not write prose sermons: he taught in **974 hymns** set to ragas. He spent his last years farming at **Kartarpur** on the Ravi, where Hindus and Muslims both claimed his body after his death in 1539.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He founded a faith now followed by about 25 to 30 million people.
spotlights.memory_hook: A guru who sang his teaching with a Muslim musician at his side.

spotlights.name: Kartarpur Sahib and the corridor

where.label: Kartarpur, Pakistan, 4.5 km from the border

spotlights.spot_it: A white gurdwara in green fields across the Ravi, visible through binoculars from a viewing platform at Dera Baba Nanak.
spotlights.story_md: Guru Nanak died at Kartarpur, which in 1947 fell on the Pakistani side, just 4.5 km from the border. For 72 years Sikhs could only gaze at the gurdwara from a platform on the Indian bank. In **November 2019**, for Nanak's 550th birth anniversary, the two countries opened the **Kartarpur Corridor**: Indian pilgrims could walk across without a visa, pay a fee, pray and eat langar, and return the same day. It was the rare thing both governments agreed on. India suspended it during COVID, reopened it in November 2021, and suspended it again on **7 May 2025** during the conflict that followed the Pahalgam attack.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a barometer of India-Pakistan relations, measured in pilgrims.
spotlights.memory_hook: Four and a half kilometres, and seventy-two years, between a people and their Guru's last home.

spotlights.name: Guru Granth Sahib
spotlights.spot_it: A large book on a cushioned platform under a canopy, with an attendant waving a whisk of yak hair over it.
spotlights.story_md: The scripture runs to **1,430 pages**, called **angs** (limbs), in the Gurmukhi script, and every printed copy has the same pagination. It is a book of **poetry and music**: almost all of it is arranged under **31 ragas**. What surprises many readers is who wrote it. Beside six of the Sikh Gurus, it includes hymns by Hindu and Muslim saints: **Kabir**, the weaver; **Ravidas**, a leatherworker from a so-called untouchable caste; **Namdev** from Maharashtra; and the Sufi **Sheikh Farid**, whose verses are among the oldest Punjabi writing anywhere. It is treated as a living Guru: it is 'put to rest' in its own room at night and carried out each morning.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the only scripture of a major religion compiled by its founders and containing saints of other faiths.
spotlights.memory_hook: A holy book that is also a songbook, and also a Guru with its own bedroom.

spotlights.name: The Khalsa, Anandpur Sahib, 1699

where.label: Takht Sri Kesgarh Sahib, Anandpur Sahib

spotlights.spot_it: A white gurdwara on a hill above the town, the place where the five beloved ones were chosen.
spotlights.story_md: On Vaisakhi in **1699**, the story goes, Guru Gobind Singh came out of a tent at Anandpur with a drawn sword and asked for a head. One man stood up and went in; the Guru returned with a bloody sword and asked again. Five men volunteered, a Khatri, a Jat, a washerman, a cook and a water-carrier, from different castes and regions. Then all five came out alive in new clothes. They were the **Panj Pyare**, the five beloved ones, baptised with sweetened water stirred with a double-edged sword. The Guru then asked them to baptise him. Men of the Khalsa took the name **Singh** (lion); women took **Kaur** (princess).
spotlights.why_it_matters: It created the Sikh identity of name, uniform and discipline seen today.
spotlights.memory_hook: Five heads asked for, five men given back: the day the lions and princesses were named.

spotlights.name: Malerkotla and the 'haah da naara'
spotlights.spot_it: A small Malwa town of mosques and a gurdwara named after a Muslim nawab's cry of protest.
spotlights.story_md: In **1705** the Mughal governor of Sirhind ordered that Guru Gobind Singh's two youngest sons, aged about **nine and six**, be bricked up alive. One man at his court objected: **Sher Mohammad Khan**, the Nawab of Malerkotla, who said the act was against Islam. His protest, the **haah da naara** (the cry of anguish), was ignored, but Sikhs never forgot it. Tradition says the Guru blessed Malerkotla. In **1947**, when massacres swept Punjab and nearly every Muslim left East Punjab, Malerkotla saw almost no killing and its Muslims stayed. It is the only Muslim-majority town in Indian Punjab and became a separate **district in 2021**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One act of conscience in 1705 is still credited with saving a town in 1947.
spotlights.memory_hook: A nawab's cry in a Mughal court became a shield for his town 242 years later.

spotlights.name: Ravidassia faith and the deras
spotlights.when: Ad Dharm movement 1925; separate faith declared 2010
spotlights.spot_it: Gurdwara-like temples with the symbol 'Har' and portraits of Guru Ravidas, packed on his birth anniversary in February.
spotlights.story_md: Almost a third of Punjab's people are Dalits, the highest share in India, and many of them felt that caste survived inside Sikh and Hindu institutions despite the teaching of the Gurus. In 1925 **Mangu Ram Mugowalia** founded the **Ad Dharm** movement, claiming a separate, pre-Aryan faith for Punjab's Dalits. Its centre today is **Dera Sachkhand Ballan** near Jalandhar. After a dera leader was murdered in Vienna in **2009**, the dera declared **Ravidassia** a separate religion in **2010**, with its own scripture, the Amritbani, drawn from Ravidas's hymns. Many Doaba Dalit families went abroad early and fund temples back home.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that caste remains a live question in a state whose faith rejected it.
spotlights.memory_hook: A cobbler-saint from Benares whose hymns sit in the Granth, and who now has a faith of his own.

sections.title: Lions of Lahore: the Sikh Empire
sections.intro_md:
After Guru Gobind Singh, Sikh power grew in the cracks of a dying Mughal empire. His follower **Banda Singh Bahadur** captured Sirhind in 1710, struck coins in the name of the Gurus and broke up big estates in favour of the peasants who tilled them, before he was captured and executed in Delhi in 1716. Sikh bands, the **misls**, then fought the Mughals and the Afghan Ahmad Shah Abdali, who blew up the Harmandir more than once.

Out of the twelve misls rose **Ranjit Singh**, who took Lahore in **1799** at the age of 19 and built an empire from the Khyber Pass to Tibet and from Kashmir to Sindh. He hired French and Italian veterans of Napoleon's wars to train one of the best armies in Asia.

He died in 1839. Within ten years his empire fell to court murders and two wars with the British, and Punjab was annexed in **1849**. South of the Sutlej, the princely states of **Patiala**, Nabha and Jind survived under British protection until 1947.

spotlights.name: Maharaja Ranjit Singh
spotlights.spot_it: In portraits: a small, one-eyed man with a long white beard, plainly dressed, often on horseback.
spotlights.story_md: Smallpox took the sight of his left eye as a child, and he never learned to read, yet Ranjit Singh became the **Sher-e-Punjab**, the Lion of Punjab. He refused the title of king for himself, ruling in the name of the Khalsa, and his court mixed Sikh, Hindu and Muslim ministers. In **1813** he obtained the **Koh-i-Noor** diamond from the exiled Afghan ruler Shah Shuja. He gilded the Harmandir and gave gold to Hindu temples at Varanasi. When he died in 1839, four queens and seven concubines were burned on his funeral pyre, a reminder that his court was not modern in every way.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He created the last major empire to resist British rule in India.
spotlights.memory_hook: One eye, no letters, and the largest diamond in the world in his armband.

spotlights.name: The Patiala Necklace
spotlights.spot_it: Five rows of platinum chain with 2,930 diamonds, and at the centre a yellow diamond the size of a golf ball.
spotlights.story_md: Maharaja **Bhupinder Singh** of Patiala (ruled 1900 to 1938) was a byword for excess: a fleet of Rolls-Royces, a private railway, and a cricket team he captained himself. In **1928** Cartier in Paris made him what is still its largest single commission: a ceremonial necklace with **2,930 diamonds**, centred on the **De Beers diamond**, about 234.6 carats, then the seventh largest in the world. It vanished from the Patiala treasury around 1948. Parts turned up in a London shop in **1998**, the big stones gone; Cartier bought the remains and rebuilt it with replica stones. Patiala also gave its name to the baggy **Patiala salwar** and the 'Patiala peg', a very large drink.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the symbol of the princely wealth of Punjab and of what was lost after 1947.
spotlights.memory_hook: A golf-ball diamond that left Patiala and came back as a copy.

sections.title: Soldiers and rebels
sections.intro_md:
After 1857, when Punjabi troops helped the British crush the uprising, the Raj declared Sikhs and Punjabi Muslims 'martial races' and recruited them in huge numbers. Punjabi soldiers fought in China, Africa, France and Mesopotamia. In 1897 at **Saragarhi**, 21 Sikh soldiers died holding a signal post against thousands of tribesmen.

The same villages produced rebels. In **1914** the ship **Komagata Maru**, carrying 376 mostly Punjabi passengers, was turned away from Vancouver under Canada's exclusion rules; when it returned to Calcutta, police fired on the passengers at Budge Budge. The **Ghadar Party**, founded by Punjabi migrants on the US Pacific coast in 1913, tried to start a revolt in the army. Then, on **13 April 1919**, came Jallianwala Bagh, and Punjab became the hottest front of the freedom struggle. Its most famous martyrs, **Bhagat Singh** and **Udham Singh**, were both in their twenties or thirties when they were hanged.

spotlights.name: Jallianwala Bagh
spotlights.spot_it: A walled garden near the Golden Temple with a flame-shaped red memorial, a narrow entrance lane and bullet holes ringed in white.
spotlights.story_md: On Vaisakhi, **13 April 1919**, thousands gathered in this enclosed ground, many of them pilgrims and families who did not know a ban on meetings was in force. Brigadier-General **Reginald Dyer** marched in troops through the only main entrance and, without warning, ordered them to fire. They shot for about ten minutes, some **1,650 rounds**, aiming where the crowd was thickest. Official figures gave **379** dead; Indian estimates ran to about **1,000**. People jumped into a well to escape; it is still there. Tagore returned his knighthood. Gandhi, who had backed the British in the war, turned against the Raj. In 2019 the British prime minister called it a 'shameful scar' but did not apologise.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turned millions of Indians from loyal subjects into opponents of British rule.
spotlights.memory_hook: One lane in, ten minutes of fire, and a well that still holds the memory.

spotlights.name: Bhagat Singh

where.label: Khatkar Kalan, Nawanshahr; executed in Lahore

spotlights.spot_it: A young man with a thin moustache, best known from a 1929 photograph in a tilted felt hat.
spotlights.story_md: Bhagat Singh was 12 when he visited Jallianwala Bagh the day after the massacre and took home soil soaked in blood. In 1928 he and comrades shot a British police officer, **John Saunders**, in Lahore to avenge the death of Lala Lajpat Rai. In **1929** he threw harmless bombs into the Central Legislative Assembly in Delhi and stayed to be arrested, to turn his trial into a stage. In jail he read hundreds of books, went on a long hunger strike, and wrote the essay **'Why I Am an Atheist'**. He was hanged in Lahore on **23 March 1931**, aged 23, with Rajguru and Sukhdev, and cremated at **Hussainiwala** on the Sutlej, where they share a memorial.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He is India's most popular revolutionary icon, claimed by the left, the right and every Punjabi.
spotlights.memory_hook: A hat, a smile, a slogan, Inquilab Zindabad, and a rope at 23.

spotlights.name: Udham Singh
spotlights.spot_it: Photographs show a slight man in a suit and hat, being led out of Caxton Hall in London by police in 1940.
spotlights.story_md: An orphan from **Sunam**, Udham Singh is said to have been near Jallianwala Bagh on the day of the massacre. He waited **21 years**. On **13 March 1940**, at a meeting in **Caxton Hall**, London, he drew a revolver hidden in a book and shot dead **Michael O'Dwyer**, who had been Punjab's governor in 1919 and had defended Dyer. At his trial he gave his name as **Ram Mohammad Singh Azad**, combining the three main faiths of Punjab and the word for freedom. He was hanged at Pentonville prison on 31 July 1940. His remains were brought back to India in **1974** and cremated at Sunam.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He became the symbol of Indian anger over Jallianwala, and of Punjab's shared Hindu, Muslim and Sikh identity.
spotlights.memory_hook: Twenty-one years, one book with a gun inside, and a name that held three faiths.

sections.title: 1947: the line through the middle
sections.intro_md:
No province suffered Partition like Punjab. The **Radcliffe Line**, drawn in five weeks by a British lawyer, **Cyril Radcliffe**, who had never been to India, was announced on **17 August 1947**, two days after independence. It put Lahore in Pakistan and Amritsar in India, 50 km apart, and cut through canals, railways, villages and family land.

What followed was one of the largest and fastest migrations in history. Across the whole subcontinent about **14 to 18 million** people moved; estimates of the dead run from about **200,000 to 2 million**, most of them in Punjab. Trains arrived carrying only corpses. Tens of thousands of women were abducted, and some families killed their own women to 'protect their honour'. Sikh and Hindu Punjabis fled east; Muslims fled west.

Refugees rebuilt fast. Families from Lahore, Rawalpindi and Lyallpur set up shops and restaurants in Delhi, Amritsar and Ludhiana, and many dishes and businesses now thought of as 'Punjabi' were refugee inventions. The old trunk road between Amritsar and Lahore is now the **Attari-Wagah** border, the only road crossing between the two countries.

spotlights.name: The Partition of Punjab
spotlights.spot_it: Black-and-white photographs of trains with people clinging to roofs, and long columns of bullock carts on dusty roads.
spotlights.story_md: Some caravans of refugees on foot and in bullock carts stretched for tens of kilometres. **Kafilas** of up to 400,000 people moved across the new border in the autumn of 1947. The violence was organised as well as spontaneous: militias attacked trains and villages on both sides. Writers carried the memory. **Saadat Hasan Manto**'s story *Toba Tek Singh* imagines an asylum where the inmates are divided like the country. **Amrita Pritam** wrote a lament to the poet Waris Shah. In 2017 the **Partition Museum** opened in Amritsar's Town Hall, the first museum anywhere dedicated to it, built largely from survivors' objects and oral histories.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It reshaped the people, food, politics and memory of Punjab on both sides.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two cities 50 km apart, and a line that took five weeks to draw and a lifetime to cross.

spotlights.name: The Attari-Wagah beating retreat
spotlights.spot_it: Tall soldiers in fan-shaped turban crests high-kicking and stamping towards the gates, while crowds cheer from stands on both sides.
spotlights.story_md: Every evening since **1959**, India's Border Security Force and the Pakistan Rangers lower their flags together at the border gate. The ceremony became a show: soldiers chosen for height march at each other, kick their legs to head height, stamp and glare, and the crowds on each side chant patriotic slogans. At the end the flags come down at the same speed, and traditionally the commanders shook hands. After the **Pahalgam attack in April 2025**, India scaled the ceremony down: the gates stayed shut and there was no handshake. Attari is also where the rail line to Lahore and the Samjhauta Express once crossed.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the one daily, public encounter between India and Pakistan.
spotlights.memory_hook: A goose-step, a glare and two flags falling together at sunset.

sections.title: Remaking the state, and the dark decade
sections.intro_md:
After 1947 Sikh leaders, led by the **Akali Dal** and **Master Tara Singh** and later **Sant Fateh Singh**, campaigned for a Punjabi-speaking state. Delhi resisted, fearing a Sikh-majority state on the border. The **Punjabi Suba** finally arrived on **1 November 1966**: the Hindi-speaking south became **Haryana**, the hills went to Himachal Pradesh, and Chandigarh was left shared and unresolved. River waters were never fully settled either; the **Sutlej-Yamuna Link canal** has been fought over for half a century.

Grievances over water, Chandigarh and Sikh identity, mixed with rivalry between the Congress and the Akali Dal, fed the rise of the preacher **Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale** and an armed movement for a separate state, **Khalistan**. In June 1984 the army stormed the Golden Temple. In October 1984 Indira Gandhi was killed by her Sikh bodyguards, and in the days that followed about **3,000** Sikhs were murdered in Delhi alone. Insurgency and counter-insurgency in Punjab killed many thousands more, militants, police and civilians, before the violence ended by about **1993**. Families of the 'disappeared' still seek answers.

spotlights.name: The Punjabi Suba, 1 November 1966
spotlights.spot_it: Old photographs of Akali volunteers marching in jathas (bands) for a Punjabi-speaking state.
spotlights.story_md: The demand was for a state drawn on language, as India had done elsewhere in 1956. Sant Fateh Singh threatened to fast unto death and burn himself; the 1965 war with Pakistan, in which Punjab bore the brunt, changed the mood in Delhi. The **Punjab Reorganisation Act** split the state on **1 November 1966**. The new Punjab had a Sikh majority for the first time, and **Punjabi in Gurmukhi** became its official language. But the deal left three sores: Chandigarh, promised to Punjab in 1970 and 1985 but never handed over; Punjabi-speaking villages left in Haryana; and the sharing of Ravi-Beas water. All three are still argued over in 2026.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It created today's Punjab and the disputes that still divide it from Haryana.
spotlights.memory_hook: 1966: a language got a state, and two states got one capital.

spotlights.name: Akal Takht and Operation Blue Star
spotlights.spot_it: A five-storey building with a gilded dome facing the Harmandir across the courtyard, the seat of Sikh temporal authority.
spotlights.story_md: Guru Hargobind built the **Akal Takht**, the Throne of the Timeless, in 1606 after his father's execution: he wore two swords, one for spiritual and one for worldly power, and the Takht faces the Harmandir to say the two belong together. In 1984 Bhindranwale fortified it. Between **1 and 8 June 1984** the army attacked with infantry and, finally, tanks. The government's figure was **493** militants and civilians and **83** soldiers killed; others put civilian deaths far higher, since pilgrims were present for a Guru's martyrdom day. The Takht was badly damaged. A government-rebuilt version was torn down by Sikhs, who rebuilt it themselves through voluntary service in the late 1980s and 1990s.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Blue Star is the deepest wound in modern Sikh memory and shaped Indian politics for decades.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two swords, one throne, and tanks in a temple courtyard in June 1984.

sections.title: The granary, and the bill
sections.intro_md:
In the mid-1960s India was importing millions of tonnes of American wheat a year, and droughts in 1965 and 1966 brought fears of famine. The answer came largely from Punjab. Dwarf wheat varieties bred by **Norman Borlaug** in Mexico, adapted by Indian scientists including **M. S. Swaminathan** and tested at **Punjab Agricultural University** in Ludhiana, could double yields if they got water and fertiliser. Punjab had both canals and farmers ready to buy tubewells. Wheat output in the state roughly tripled within a decade.

Then came rice. Punjabis traditionally ate little rice, but guaranteed government purchase, the **minimum support price**, made **paddy** in summer and wheat in winter the safest income in India. Since 1997 Punjab has given farmers **free electricity** for their pumps. The result is a state with about 1.5% of India's area that grows about **17%** of its wheat and **12%** of its rice, and the most intensively farmed land in the country.

The bill is now due. The water table under most of the state is falling by roughly half a metre to a metre a year, and the Central Ground Water Board classes about three-quarters of Punjab's 150-odd blocks as **over-exploited**.

spotlights.name: The Green Revolution in wheat
spotlights.spot_it: Endless short golden wheat in April, cut by combine harvesters, and grain piled in open mandis under tarpaulin.
spotlights.story_md: In **1966** India imported about **18,000 tonnes** of Mexican dwarf wheat seed, the largest seed purchase in the world at that time. The old tall Punjabi wheat fell over when fertilised heavily; the new short-stemmed plants held up their heavy heads. **Punjab Agricultural University**, founded in **1962** and modelled on American land-grant universities, ran trials and spread the seeds through extension workers and farmer fairs. By about 1970, Punjab was feeding a large share of the national grain stock, and India had stopped begging for food aid. Borlaug won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970. In Punjab, a generation of farmers became prosperous, and bought tractors, motorcycles and tubewells.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It ended India's dependence on food aid, and Punjab did the most to make it happen.
spotlights.memory_hook: A short wheat plant from Mexico that stood up straight and saved India from begging.

spotlights.name: Paddy and the falling water table
spotlights.spot_it: Flooded green rice fields in the June heat, and tubewell pumps gushing into brick channels.
spotlights.story_md: One kilogram of rice can take **3,000 to 5,000 litres** of water, and Punjab plants about 3 million hectares of it in the hottest, driest months. Free power means no one pays for pumping, so tubewells have gone deeper and deeper; many now need expensive submersible pumps. In 2009 the state passed the **Punjab Preservation of Subsoil Water Act**, which bans transplanting paddy before mid-June, when evaporation is lower. It slowed the decline but pushed the rice harvest later, leaving less time to clear fields for wheat. Experts have warned for years that some aquifers in central Punjab could be largely exhausted within a few decades.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Punjab is effectively exporting its groundwater to the rest of India in every sack of rice.
spotlights.memory_hook: Every kilogram of rice leaves Punjab carrying a bathtub's worth of its water, many times over.

spotlights.name: Stubble burning
spotlights.spot_it: Rows of fires and black smoke rising from harvested rice fields at dusk in October.
spotlights.story_md: Machines harvest paddy in October but leave tall stubble, and farmers have perhaps three weeks before they must sow wheat. Burning is the cheapest way to clear it. Satellite fire counts in Punjab ran into the tens of thousands in many years, about **36,600** in 2023, before falling to about **10,900** in 2024, helped by subsidised machines such as the **Happy Seeder**, which sows wheat straight into the stubble. The smoke drifts south-east, adding to Delhi's winter smog, though studies differ on how much of Delhi's pollution it causes. Farmers argue that they burn because the system, not they, chose paddy.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It links a farming system to the air of north India.
spotlights.memory_hook: The smoke of Punjab's harvest is part of what Delhi breathes in November.

spotlights.name: The farmers' protest, 2020 to 2021
spotlights.spot_it: Tractor-trolleys turned into homes along the highways into Delhi, with langars, libraries and laundries.
spotlights.story_md: In September 2020 Parliament passed three farm laws to open up crop trading. Punjab's farmers feared the end of guaranteed purchase. From **November 2020** tens of thousands camped at Delhi's borders, at **Singhu** and Tikri, through a freezing winter and a COVID summer. The camps were a small city: langars, libraries, free medical tents, a newspaper and even foot-massage machines. Hundreds of protesters died during the year, by the unions' count. On **19 November 2021**, Guru Nanak's birthday, the prime minister announced the laws would be repealed. It was one of the largest and longest protests in Indian history, led largely by Punjab.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It showed how much Punjab's economy and identity depend on the state's role in buying its grain.
spotlights.memory_hook: A year on the highway with tractors, langars and libraries, and three laws undone.

sections.title: Punjabi: one language, two scripts
sections.intro_md:
Punjabi is spoken by well over **100 million** people, most of them in Pakistan, which makes it one of the ten or so most spoken languages on Earth. In India, Census 2011 counted about **33 million** speakers. It is an Indo-Aryan language with a rare feature among its relatives: it is **tonal**. A letter that once marked a breathy sound, such as the *gh* in older spellings, now changes the pitch of the vowel instead, so *koṛā* can mean a whip or a leper depending on the tone.

In India it is written in **Gurmukhi**, 'from the mouth of the Guru'; in Pakistan, in **Shahmukhi**, a version of the Perso-Arabic script. The same poem can look entirely different on either side of the border and sound the same.

Punjabi literature begins with the Sufi **Baba Farid** in the 12th and 13th centuries, runs through the Gurus and the qissa poets who told long love stories in verse, and reaches modern times with **Amrita Pritam** and **Shiv Kumar Batalvi**. Its film and music industry now reaches Canada, Britain and Australia as much as Ludhiana.

spotlights.name: Gurmukhi script
spotlights.spot_it: Letters that hang from a flat headline like Devanagari but with rounder shapes; the first letter is ੳ, which looks like a hook.
spotlights.story_md: Tradition credits the second Guru, **Angad** (Guru 1539 to 1552), with standardising a script from the merchants' shorthand of Punjab so that ordinary people could read the Gurus' hymns without Brahmin intermediaries. The classic alphabet has **35 letters**, the paintī; a few more with dots were added later for Persian and English sounds. The Guru Granth Sahib is written in it, which is why Sikhs see the script itself as sacred. Since 1966 it has been the official script of Punjab, where shop signs must carry Gurmukhi on top. Unicode added it in 1991, and Punjabi University, Patiala, has spent decades building fonts and software for it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It ties a language, a religion and a state together in one alphabet.
spotlights.memory_hook: An alphabet named 'from the Guru's mouth', made so that farmers could read God's songs.

spotlights.name: Heer Ranjha, by Waris Shah
spotlights.spot_it: Recited, not read: long rhymed verses sung at fairs and weddings, often starting with Heer by the river Chenab.
spotlights.story_md: Heer is the beautiful daughter of a rich family in **Jhang**; Ranjha, a younger son who has fallen out with his brothers, becomes her father's cowherd and plays the flute. They fall in love, she is forced to marry another man, he becomes a wandering jogi to reach her, and the story ends with poison and death. Many poets told it, but **Waris Shah**'s version of **1766** became the classic, full of earthy proverbs and village life. It is to Punjabi what Shakespeare is to English: people quote it without knowing they are doing so. Heer's tomb in Jhang is visited by lovers, and every Punjabi love song carries a trace of it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the defining love story of Punjab on both sides of the border.
spotlights.memory_hook: A cowherd's flute, a forced marriage, poisoned sweets: Punjab's Romeo and Juliet.

spotlights.name: Amrita Pritam
spotlights.spot_it: A woman with large dark eyes and a cigarette in old photographs, often next to the painter Imroz.
spotlights.story_md: In 1947, on a train from Lahore to Dehradun, Amrita Pritam wrote **'Ajj aakhaan Waris Shah nu'** (Today I call on Waris Shah): you wrote a whole epic for one weeping daughter of Punjab; today a hundred thousand daughters weep, rise from your grave and write. It became the elegy of Partition on both sides. She was the first woman to win the **Sahitya Akademi Award** (1956) and later won the **Jnanpith** (1981). She wrote about 100 books, including the Partition novel *Pinjar*. Her private life was bold for her time: she left her marriage and lived for 40 years with the artist **Imroz**, who painted her book covers.
spotlights.why_it_matters: She is the voice of women's suffering in Partition and a pioneer of Indian women's writing.
spotlights.memory_hook: One poem to a dead poet that spoke for a hundred thousand living women.

sections.title: Dhol, bhangra and the global Punjabi beat
sections.intro_md:
Punjabi music lives on two tracks. One is devotional: **kirtan**, the singing of the Guru Granth Sahib's hymns in ragas, live day and night from the Golden Temple, where professional singers called **ragis** have performed in rotation since the Gurus' time. The other is earthy: folk songs for harvest, weddings and wrestling matches, carried by the booming **dhol**, the one-stringed **tumbi** and the twin flutes of the **algoza**.

The folk side went global through migration. In 1970s and 1980s Britain, Punjabi bands in Birmingham and Southall mixed bhangra with disco and reggae. **Panjabi MC**'s *Mundian To Bach Ke* (1998) became a worldwide hit in 2003 with a Jay-Z remix. Today Punjabi pop is one of India's biggest musical exports, streamed in Canada, the US, Britain and Australia. Its stars include **Diljit Dosanjh**, who sold out stadiums worldwide, and **Sidhu Moose Wala**, shot dead in 2022.

Critics point to a darker side: many hits celebrate guns, drugs and caste pride, and Punjab's government has tried, with little success, to curb songs that glorify weapons.

spotlights.name: Bhangra
spotlights.spot_it: Men in bright turbans and loose kurtas with lungis, arms raised, shoulders bouncing, jumping to a dhol beat.
spotlights.story_md: Bhangra began as a men's dance at the **wheat harvest** around Vaisakhi, especially in Sialkot and Gujranwala, now in Pakistan. After Partition, troupes in Indian Punjab turned it into a stage dance, adding steps from other folk dances, and it became the face of Punjab at Republic Day parades. The engine is the **dhol**, a barrel drum hung from the shoulder and struck with a thick stick on one side and a thin cane on the other, in the 'chaal' rhythm. Dancers shout **'balle balle'** and **'hoi'**. Props include the **saap**, a wooden lattice that snaps open and shut. The fitness world has borrowed it as 'Bhangra workout'.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the best-known dance from India outside India.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two hands to the sky, one dhol in the gut, and the wheat is in.

spotlights.name: Giddha
spotlights.spot_it: A circle of women in bright suits and phulkari, clapping in rhythm while two dancers step into the middle and act out a short sung verse.
spotlights.story_md: Giddha is the women's answer to bhangra, and in some ways the sharper one. It needs no drum: the rhythm comes from **clapping**, sometimes with a small pot, the gharha. One woman sings a **boli**, a short couplet, and the others repeat the last line while a pair dances it out in mime. Bolis are witty and often cheeky: they tease husbands, complain about mothers-in-law, mock village gossips and talk frankly about love. At weddings and at **Teeyan**, the monsoon festival when married women return to their parents' villages, giddha was one of the few spaces where women could say what they thought, in public, in verse.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It preserves a tradition of women's satire and protest in song.
spotlights.memory_hook: No drum, just hands and a boli about the mother-in-law.

spotlights.name: Diljit Dosanjh
spotlights.spot_it: A singer in a neat turban and designer clothes, often in sunglasses, singing in Punjabi to stadium crowds.
spotlights.story_md: Diljit Dosanjh grew up singing kirtan in gurdwaras in Ludhiana and became a Punjabi pop and film star in the 2000s. In **April 2023** he became the first Punjabi artist to headline a set at **Coachella** in California, opening with 'Punjabi aa gaye oye'. His **Dil-Luminati** tour in 2024 sold out arenas in North America, Europe and India. In **2025** he made his Met Gala debut in an outfit modelled on the **Maharaja of Patiala**, with a replica of the Patiala necklace. His success, as a turbaned Sikh singing only in Punjabi, is often cited as proof that Indian regional pop no longer needs Hindi or English to go global.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He is the most visible face of Punjabi culture worldwide today.
spotlights.memory_hook: A turban at Coachella, and the Patiala necklace on the Met Gala steps.

sections.title: Phulkari, juttis and the turban
sections.intro_md:
Punjab's crafts grew out of village homes. Women embroidered **phulkari** shawls for weddings; leather-workers made embroidered **juttis**; the **thatheras** of Jandiala Guru hammered brass and copper vessels. Dress was practical for farm work and festive for weddings: for women, the **salwar kameez** with a **dupatta**, now worn across India, and the **paranda**, a coloured silk tassel braided into the hair; for men, the **kurta** and the **tehmat** or lungi, and the turban.

The turban, **dastar** or **pagg**, is the most visible sign of Punjab worldwide. For Sikhs it is an article of faith covering uncut hair, the **kesh**, one of the **Five Ks** along with the comb (kangha), steel bracelet (kara), sword (kirpan) and undershorts (kachera). Punjabi Hindus and Muslims also wore turbans in the past. Styles and colours carry meaning: the tall, peaked **Patiala shahi** style, the round Nihang turbans with steel quoits, and saffron or blue for religious occasions.

spotlights.name: Phulkari
spotlights.spot_it: Coarse handspun cotton, usually rust red, almost hidden under bright silk darning stitches in yellow, orange and pink, worked in geometric patterns.
spotlights.story_md: Phulkari means 'flower work'. It is embroidered from the **back** of the cloth with darning stitches in untwisted silk floss called **pat**, counting threads instead of tracing a pattern, so the motifs are geometric. When the embroidery covers the entire cloth so that no base shows, it is called a **bagh**, a garden. A grandmother would begin a bagh at a girl's birth and the family would add to it until her wedding, when she wore it. Old phulkaris have hidden 'mistakes' stitched in to ward off the evil eye. Phulkari received a **Geographical Indication** tag in **2011**, covering Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan. Museum pieces now sell for thousands of dollars.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is Punjab's signature textile and a record of women's unpaid art.
spotlights.memory_hook: A garden stitched from the back over twenty years, for one wedding day.

spotlights.name: The Thatheras of Jandiala Guru
spotlights.spot_it: A narrow lane full of rhythmic hammering, men tapping big brass and copper pots on iron anvils, the metal covered in tiny dimples.
spotlights.story_md: The thatheras are a community of metalworkers who settled at **Jandiala Guru** near Amritsar, encouraged by Maharaja Ranjit Singh. They heat brass and copper sheets and beat them into shape by hand, and finish them with a pattern of tiny **hammer marks** that is their signature. Their pots, called **patila**, **gaagar** and **parat**, were once part of every Punjabi kitchen and dowry, and many are used in gurdwara langars. In **2014** UNESCO put their craft on its list of the **Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity**. Steel and plastic have shrunk demand, and only a few families still work in the craft.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is Punjab's only craft on UNESCO's intangible heritage list.
spotlights.memory_hook: A lane where every pot carries a thousand hammer blows, and UNESCO noticed.

sections.title: Ghee, wheat and the tandoor
sections.intro_md:
Punjabi food is wheat country food: rotis rather than rice, ghee and butter on everything, buttermilk in steel tumblers, and heavy winter dishes built for a day in the fields. Villages once shared a **sanjha chulha**, a communal clay oven where women brought dough to be baked into rotis, a social space as much as a kitchen.

The home table is simpler than the restaurant version. Daily dishes are **dal** (often black urad and rajma), seasonal greens, fresh white cheese (**paneer**), curd, pickles and lots of buttermilk (**lassi** or **chhachh**). Meat is eaten more in some communities than others; many Sikh and Hindu households are vegetarian, and alcohol, especially whisky, is common in many homes despite religious disapproval.

Much of the 'Punjabi food' sold in Indian restaurants worldwide, such as **butter chicken** and **tandoori chicken**, actually comes from the Punjabi refugees of **1947** who opened eateries in Delhi. That food then travelled with the diaspora to Southall, Brampton and Melbourne.

spotlights.name: Sarson da saag and makki di roti
spotlights.spot_it: A thick dark-green mash of mustard leaves topped with a lump of white butter, eaten with a yellow, slightly crumbly maize flatbread.
spotlights.story_md: Sarson da saag is made from **mustard greens**, often mixed with spinach and bathua, cooked for hours with ginger, garlic and green chilli, then mashed with a wooden stick called a **ghotna** and thickened with a little maize flour. It tastes better the next day. It is eaten with **makki di roti**, flatbread of maize flour that is hard to roll because the dough has no gluten, so women pat it out by hand. A dollop of white homemade butter goes on top, with jaggery and a glass of lassi on the side. It is a winter dish: the yellow mustard fields that bloom in January are one of the iconic sights of rural Punjab.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the dish most Punjabis name as their home food.
spotlights.memory_hook: Green saag, yellow roti, white butter: a Punjabi winter on a plate.

spotlights.name: Butter chicken and the tandoor
spotlights.spot_it: Orange, creamy tomato gravy with pieces of tandoori chicken, with a swirl of cream on top.
spotlights.story_md: The story most often told: **Kundan Lal Gujral**, a refugee who had run a restaurant in **Peshawar**, opened **Moti Mahal** in Delhi's Daryaganj after Partition. He brought the **tandoor**, a clay oven sunk into the ground that in Punjab was mainly for bread, and used it to cook spiced chicken. Leftover tandoori chicken dried out, so the kitchen simmered it in a sauce of tomato, butter and cream. That was butter chicken, or **murgh makhani**. A rival restaurant group, Daryaganj, has argued in the Delhi High Court since **2024** that its founder, Kundan Lal Jaggi, was the co-inventor. The case is unresolved.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most famous Indian dish in the world, and it was born of Partition.
spotlights.memory_hook: A refugee, a clay oven and a pot of leftover chicken: the world's favourite curry.

sections.title: Harvests, bonfires and mock battles
sections.intro_md:
Punjab's calendar follows the two harvests and the lives of the Gurus. **Lohri** in January marks the end of the coldest nights and the growth of the winter crop. **Vaisakhi** in April celebrates the wheat harvest and the founding of the Khalsa. **Hola Mohalla** follows Holi with martial games at Anandpur Sahib. **Teeyan** brings women together in the monsoon month of Sawan. **Bandi Chhor Divas**, on the same day as Diwali, celebrates Guru Hargobind's release from Gwalior Fort, and the Golden Temple is lit with lamps and fireworks.

**Gurpurabs**, the birth and martyrdom anniversaries of the Gurus, are marked with processions called **nagar kirtans**: the Guru Granth Sahib is carried through the streets on a decorated float, led by five men representing the Panj Pyare, while volunteers sweep the road ahead and hand out food.

There is also a sports festival: the **Kila Raipur** 'Rural Olympics', held near Ludhiana since **1933**, with races, strongman contests and tractor stunts.

data.name: Bandi Chhor Divas (with Diwali), Guru Nanak Gurpurab

spotlights.name: Vaisakhi
spotlights.spot_it: Golden wheat fields ready for harvest, fairs with bhangra, and saffron flags at gurdwaras.
spotlights.story_md: Vaisakhi falls on **13 or 14 April**, the start of the solar month of Vaisakh. For farmers it is the signal that the wheat is ripe; for Sikhs it is the anniversary of the founding of the Khalsa in **1699**. Gurdwaras hold special prayers and replace the cloth on the tall flagpole, the **Nishan Sahib**. Large fairs are held at **Talwandi Sabo** (Damdama Sahib), Anandpur and Amritsar. The date carries other memories too: the Jallianwala Bagh massacre happened on Vaisakhi in 1919. Abroad, Vaisakhi parades in **Surrey**, British Columbia, and other Canadian cities have drawn crowds of several hundred thousand, among the largest Sikh gatherings outside India.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It joins the farm year, the faith and the diaspora in one day.
spotlights.memory_hook: Wheat ripe, flags changed, and a parade in Canada bigger than many Punjab towns.

spotlights.name: Lohri
spotlights.spot_it: A bonfire at night with families circling it and throwing in sesame, peanuts, popcorn and rewri (sesame-jaggery sweets).
spotlights.story_md: Lohri is celebrated on the night of **13 January**, the eve of Makar Sankranti, as the winter crop grows and the nights begin to shorten. Children go from house to house singing and asking for sweets and firewood; the song most often sung, **'Sunder mundriye'**, praises **Dulla Bhatti**, a 16th-century Punjabi Muslim outlaw who rebelled against Akbar and was remembered for rescuing girls being sold and arranging their marriages. Families with a new bride or baby hold a big Lohri. In recent decades many families have begun celebrating a daughter's first Lohri as well as a son's, a small cultural correction in a state with a skewed sex ratio.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the warmest night of Punjabi winter, and the memory of a Muslim folk hero.
spotlights.memory_hook: A bonfire, a song for an outlaw, and popcorn thrown into the flames.

spotlights.name: Hola Mohalla
spotlights.spot_it: Nihang Sikhs in blue robes and tall turbans riding horses standing up, sparring with swords and spears.
spotlights.story_md: Guru Gobind Singh turned the colour festival of Holi into a day of **martial practice** around 1701, with mock battles at Anandpur. Hola Mohalla continues it. The stars are the **Nihangs**, an order of Sikh warriors in deep blue robes and towering turbans wrapped with steel quoits (**chakkars**) and small weapons. They show **gatka** (stick and sword fighting), ride two horses at once, and pick up tent pegs at a gallop. Hundreds of thousands of pilgrims come, and the langars along the roads run for three days. In some recent years, groups have also been criticised for unruly behaviour and stunts on the roads.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It keeps alive the warrior side of Sikh tradition.
spotlights.memory_hook: Holi without the colours: horses, swords and blue turbans as tall as a child.

sections.title: Hockey villages, flying Sikhs and the kabaddi circle
sections.intro_md:
For a state of under 3 crore people, Punjab has produced a remarkable share of India's sportspeople, especially in **hockey**, athletics, wrestling, weightlifting and shooting. The farm diet of milk and ghee, the army's sports programmes and village rivalry all helped. The town of **Jalandhar** makes a large share of India's sports goods, from hockey sticks to cricket balls, an industry started by refugees from **Sialkot** in 1947.

The Indian hockey teams that won Olympic gold were full of Punjabis, and so was the team that won **bronze at Tokyo 2020** under captain **Manpreet Singh** of Mithapur, Jalandhar. **Dara Singh** from a village near Amritsar became a world wrestling champion, a film star and, in the 1987 TV *Ramayan*, Hanuman. Village akharas still train young wrestlers in mud pits.

The local game is **circle kabaddi**, played on a round field, with stars who are celebrities in the diaspora and a long history of tournaments funded by NRIs.

spotlights.name: Milkha Singh, the Flying Sikh
spotlights.spot_it: A lean runner in a white vest with a long-hair top knot (joora) and a headband, mid-stride.
spotlights.story_md: Milkha Singh was a teenager when his parents and several siblings were killed in Partition violence. He escaped to Delhi, lived in refugee camps, and joined the army, where he discovered running. He won gold at the 1958 Commonwealth Games, India's first. At the **1960 Rome Olympics** he finished **fourth** in the 400 m by a fraction of a second, in **45.73** seconds, an Indian record that stood for **38 years**. Pakistan's president Ayub Khan named him the **Flying Sikh** after he beat Pakistan's best sprinter in Lahore in 1960. He died of COVID in **June 2021**. The 2013 film *Bhaag Milkha Bhaag* told his story.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He was India's first global track star and a symbol of rising from Partition.
spotlights.memory_hook: Fourth in Rome by a hair, first in the hearts of two countries.

spotlights.name: Sansarpur, the hockey village
spotlights.spot_it: A small village next to the Jalandhar army cantonment with a hockey ground and a gallery of old team photographs.
spotlights.story_md: Sansarpur has produced about **14 Olympic hockey players**, most for India but also four for **Kenya** and one for **Canada**, carried abroad by Punjabi migration. In **1968** seven players from this one village took part in the Mexico City Olympics, five for India and two for Kenya. The village grew up beside the army cantonment, where British regiments played hockey and local boys picked up the game on its grounds. Its story is matched by others: **Balbir Singh Senior**, born near Moga, won three Olympic golds and scored **five goals** in the 1952 final, a record that still stands. Today, Sansarpur's grounds are often neglected, and the cricket age has taken over.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how deep Punjab's roots in Indian hockey go.
spotlights.memory_hook: One village, two continents' teams, seven Olympians in the same Games.

sections.title: Villages, dreams of abroad, and a water tank shaped like a plane
sections.intro_md:
Most Punjabis still live in villages, about 63% in 2011, but rural Punjab is unlike most of India. Roads are paved, nearly every village has electricity and a gurdwara, and large brick houses, called **kothis**, stand next to fields. Land is the core of status, especially for the **Jat Sikh** farming caste, which owns most of it, while Dalit families, about a third of the population, own very little.

The great outlet is migration. Punjabis went to East Africa, Malaysia, Britain and North America from the late 19th century. Today the dream of going abroad, **bahar jaana**, shapes whole districts: towns are full of **IELTS** coaching centres and visa agents, and families mortgage land to send children to Canada or Australia as students. Some take the illegal **'donkey route'** through Latin America to the US; in **February 2025**, US military planes deported more than 100 Indians, many of them Punjabis, in handcuffs.

The flip side is empty villages, old parents alone in big houses, and a fear among Punjab's politicians that the state is losing its young.

spotlights.name: Rooftop water tank sculptures
spotlights.spot_it: A concrete water tank on a village roof shaped like an aeroplane, an eagle, a football or a tractor.
spotlights.story_md: Drive through Doaba and you will see aeroplanes parked on rooftops: they are **water tanks**. Families whose members went abroad, often the first to fly, began building tanks shaped as **planes**, and the idea spread to footballs, eagles, horses, ships, tractors and even a hockey player, each said to reflect something about the family. Plane tanks became so common in certain villages that the area was nicknamed after them. They are a kind of folk sculpture of migration: a way to tell the neighbours that someone in this house made it to London or Toronto. Some families even put the airline name on the wing.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They are the most visible sign of how emigration has reshaped village Punjab.
spotlights.memory_hook: A plane on the roof that never takes off, because the son already did.

spotlights.name: Punjab abroad: Brampton, Surrey and Southall
spotlights.spot_it: A Canadian suburb where shop signs are in Gurmukhi, gurdwaras have parking lots, and the Vaisakhi parade fills the streets.
spotlights.story_md: The first Sikh soldiers passed through Canada in **1897** on their way home from Queen Victoria's jubilee, and some returned to work in British Columbia's sawmills. Despite racist exclusion laws, such as the one that turned back the Komagata Maru in 1914, the community grew. Today **Punjabi** is one of the most spoken languages in Canada after English and French, with about **940,000** speakers in the 2021 census, and Sikhs have served as Canadian cabinet ministers. Brampton near Toronto and Surrey near Vancouver are among the most Punjabi cities outside India. In Britain the heart of the community is **Southall** in west London.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The diaspora shapes Punjab's economy, music, politics and its relations with other countries.
spotlights.memory_hook: More Punjabi on a Brampton shop sign than on a Delhi one.

sections.title: Places to go
sections.intro_md:
Most visitors see Amritsar: the Golden Temple at dawn and after dark, the Jallianwala Bagh, the Partition Museum, the old walled city's food lanes and the evening ceremony at Attari. Plan on at least two days.

Beyond it, Punjab rewards slower travel. **Anandpur Sahib**, below the Shivalik hills, holds the Takht Kesgarh Sahib and the **Virasat-e-Khalsa** museum. **Patiala** has the **Qila Mubarak** and the Sheesh Mahal with mirror-work rooms. **Bathinda** has its brick fort, and **Kapurthala**, a former princely state, has a palace modelled on Versailles, now a military school. Birders go to **Harike** in winter. Food lovers go to Amritsar and to Ludhiana's dhabas.

Chandigarh, the shared capital, is the gateway: the Capitol Complex, the leafy **Sukhna Lake**, and Nek Chand's strange and wonderful **Rock Garden**. The best months are **October to March**; summers in the plains often go above 45°C.

spotlights.name: Nek Chand's Rock Garden
spotlights.spot_it: Thousands of figures, people, animals, dancers, made from broken bangles, crockery, tiles and electrical waste, lining a maze of courtyards and waterfalls.
spotlights.story_md: **Nek Chand Saini** was a road inspector for Chandigarh's public works department. In **1957** he began, in his spare time and in secret, to build figures from the waste of the new city: broken toilets, bangles, crockery, tiles and stones, in a patch of forest set aside as a protected zone. When officials found it in **1975**, it already covered about 12 acres. It was illegal, but instead of demolishing it, the city put Nek Chand on a salary and opened it in **1976**. It now covers about 40 acres and draws thousands of visitors a day. Nek Chand died in **2015**, and his figures are in museums around the world.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of the largest outsider art environments in the world, and a lesson in recycling.
spotlights.memory_hook: A road inspector's secret, built from a city's garbage, became its favourite park.

sections.title: How Punjab earns, and what is happening now
sections.intro_md:
Punjab was India's richest state by income per person for much of the 1980s and 1990s. Since then it has slipped. Its per capita income is now above the national average but well behind states such as Haryana, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, and its government debt is among the highest in India relative to the size of its economy, close to half of state GDP.

Agriculture still employs a large share of workers. Industry is mostly small and medium: **Ludhiana** makes bicycles, hosiery, woollens and auto parts; **Jalandhar** makes sports goods and leather; **Mandi Gobindgarh** is a steel town; and **Mohali** has an IT and start-up cluster.

In 2022 the **Aam Aadmi Party** won **92 of 117** seats, ending decades of Congress and Akali Dal rule, and the former comedian **Bhagwant Mann** became chief minister. In **March 2025** the government launched a campaign called **Yudh Nashian Virudh** (war against drugs), with mass arrests and demolitions of the houses of alleged dealers, criticised by some as heavy-handed. The **August and September 2025** floods hit about 1,400 villages and some 3,70,000 acres of farmland. The next assembly election is due by early **2027**.

spotlights.name: Ludhiana and the bicycle
spotlights.spot_it: A dense industrial city on the Sutlej, with workshops, hosiery mills and tens of thousands of bicycles a day rolling out of factories.
spotlights.story_md: Ludhiana is Punjab's largest city, with about 1.6 million people in 2011, and its industrial engine. In **1956** four **Munjal** brothers, refugees from Kamalia in what became Pakistan, began making bicycle parts and then whole bicycles here under the name **Hero**. By **1986** Hero Cycles was listed by Guinness as the **world's largest bicycle maker** by volume, and the family went on to create Hero Honda, later Hero MotoCorp, one of the world's largest makers of motorcycles. Ludhiana also knits most of India's woollen sweaters. It pays a price: the **Buddha Nullah**, a stream through the city, is one of the most polluted water bodies in Punjab.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the proof that Punjab's refugees built an industrial economy alongside farming.
spotlights.memory_hook: Refugee brothers, a bicycle and a Guinness record, all in Ludhiana.

spotlights.name: The floods of 2025
spotlights.spot_it: Flooded paddy fields reaching the roofs of village houses, with boats where roads used to be.
spotlights.story_md: In **August and September 2025**, extremely heavy rain in Himachal Pradesh and Jammu and Kashmir filled the **Bhakra**, **Pong** and **Ranjit Sagar** reservoirs, and releases from them sent the Sutlej, Beas and Ravi over their banks. About **1,400** villages were flooded, around **55** people died, and over **3,70,000 acres** of farmland were submerged just before harvest. It was described as the worst flooding in Punjab since **1988**. The state paid ₹20,000 an acre to affected farmers. As always, gurdwaras, Sikh charities and diaspora groups ran langars and boat rescues. The disaster set off an argument about how the dams were managed and about building on floodplains.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It showed how the dams that made the Green Revolution can also flood the plain.
spotlights.memory_hook: 1988 and 2025: the rivers reminded Punjab who drew the five waters.

sections.title: Myths, and Punjab in ten lines
sections.intro_md:
**Myth: all Punjabis are Sikhs.** In Indian Punjab, 58% are Sikhs and 38% Hindus, and most Punjabi speakers in the world are Muslims in Pakistan. **Myth: butter chicken is an ancient Punjabi dish.** It was created in Delhi after 1947. **Myth: Punjab is India's richest state.** It was, in the 1980s and 1990s; it is now in the middle of the pack, with heavy debt. **Myth: the Golden Temple is solid gold.** It is copper and marble covered in gold leaf.

**In short:** five rivers, now three in India. 1.5% of India's land, 17% of its wheat. 58% Sikh, 32% Dalit. A faith of equality, served daily at the langar. An empire, then the Raj's recruiting ground, then the heart of the freedom struggle. Split in 1947, cut in 1966, wounded in 1984. A granary running out of groundwater, and a people who took Punjab to the world.

best_facts.why_surprising: A moral act repaid over 242 years.

best_facts.fact: Alexander the Great's conquest ended at the Beas in 326 BCE, when his own soldiers refused to go further.
best_facts.why_surprising: The edge of the ancient world's greatest empire runs through Punjab.

best_facts.fact: The tiny village of Sansarpur has produced about 14 Olympic hockey players, for India, Kenya and Canada; seven of them played at the 1968 Games.

side_dish.title: How an aquifer empties: the water under Punjab
side_dish.body_md:
Groundwater is not an underground lake. It is water held in the tiny spaces between grains of sand, silt and gravel, the way a sponge holds water. A layer that holds and passes enough water to supply a well is called an **aquifer**. Under Punjab, the rivers have laid down hundreds of metres of such sediment, which is why a tubewell almost anywhere used to strike water within a few metres.

An aquifer is a bank account. Rain and seepage from rivers and canals are the deposits, called **recharge**. Wells are the withdrawals. When withdrawals match deposits, the **water table**, the top of the saturated zone, stays level. When pumping exceeds recharge year after year, the table falls. The water being pumped in many Malwa districts today may have taken centuries to accumulate.

The Central Ground Water Board measures this as the **stage of extraction**: withdrawals as a percentage of annual recharge. Above 100%, a block is called **over-exploited**. Punjab as a whole has been around 160% in recent assessments, the highest of any state. Deeper water is also often saltier or carries more arsenic and uranium. Fixing it means pumping less, not just recharging more: growing less paddy, pricing power, or switching to crops like maize, pulses and cotton.

offline_task.title: Make a glass of proper Punjabi lassi, then a langar-style dal
offline_task.body_md:
**Lassi (2 glasses, 5 minutes)**
- 2 cups thick plain curd, cold
- 1/2 cup chilled water or milk
- 3 to 4 teaspoons sugar (or a pinch of salt and roasted cumin for the salty version)
- A few crushed ice cubes

Whisk hard, or blend for 30 seconds, until frothy. Pour into tall glasses. If you have cream, spoon a thick layer on top: that is the Amritsar touch.

**Langar-style dal (serves 4, 1 hour)**
- 1 cup whole black urad and 1/4 cup chana dal, soaked 2 hours
- 1 onion, 2 tomatoes, a 3 cm piece of ginger, 4 garlic cloves, 2 green chillies, all chopped
- 2 tablespoons ghee, 1 teaspoon cumin, salt, turmeric, red chilli powder

1. Pressure-cook the dals with salt and turmeric in 4 cups of water until very soft, about 6 whistles.
2. Heat ghee, add cumin, then onion, ginger, garlic and chilli until golden. Add tomato and chilli powder and cook until the ghee separates.
3. Pour the tadka into the dal, simmer 15 minutes, mashing a little.

Eat it sitting on the floor, with someone you would not usually share a meal with. That is the point of langar.
